action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). ## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for reading and writing to .pen files and gives you tools to be an expert design generator and validator specifically for web and mobile applications and websites.

- IMPORTANT: The contents of the .pen files are encrypted and can be only access via the "pencil" MCP tools. DO NOT use "Read" or "Grep" tools to read contents of .pen files.

1	# UX-02 — Conversation reader: implemented contract and evidence
2	
3	Status: implemented at the component/shell level. The six repository gates,
4	reader Chrome suite, and covered-surface focus suite pass; an existing
5	locale-sensitive row-layout assertion is recorded separately below, not hidden
6	as an unconditional green browser gate. Real-Chrome runs cover the reader
7	journey, scroll/anchor behavior, and covered-surface focus safety in the
8	synthetic browser preview only. Native fixture/WKWebView,
9	VoiceOver/assistive-technology, and platform clipboard verification remain
10	**explicitly pending**. Browser passes do not establish native IPC/provider
11	correctness or Superhuman fidelity.
12	
13	Grounding: `docs/superhuman-browsing-implementation-plan.md` (UX-02; acceptance
14	complete BROWSE-05 and the copy portion of BROWSE-15) and the UX-02 section of
15	`superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md` (message focus/expansion, participant
16	details, copy-only contact controls, reader scrolling).
17	
18	## Bounded UX-02 contract
19	
20	Implemented behavior:
21	
22	- **Visit-scoped message state** inside the mounted reader
23	  (`src/components/ReaderView.vue`), keyed by account+conversation reference and
24	  message ID — never array position. Per visit: active message ID, expanded IDs,
25	  details-disclosure state, and a viewport-relative scroll anchor with a
26	  `scrollTop` fallback. State survives J/K round trips and same-reference
27	  background replacements for the life of the mounted reader session and is
28	  released when the reader unmounts (close) or the account changes. Removed
29	  message IDs are pruned; a removed active/anchor ID resolves to the next
30	  surviving old neighbor, then the previous one. The resolved active ID is
31	  published to App so contact context follows the same surviving message as
32	  DOM focus. Empty/error states have an article fallback; loading retains saved
33	  visit state without exposing a stale message-command target.
34	- **Initial focus/expansion:** opening a conversation focuses the newest cached
35	  message's toggle (not the article) with that message expanded; only as much of
36	  its header as needed is revealed. Ordinary `ol/li` semantics with a roving
37	  primary message-toggle button carrying `aria-expanded`/`aria-controls`;
38	  focusing any control of a message updates its message identity.
39	- **Message movement (nonwrapping):** `N`/`P` move message focus one step
40	  without auto-expanding (clamped at both ends, no wrap). `O` toggles expansion
41	  of the focused message; `Shift+O` idempotently expands all messages. These are
42	  narrow methods exposed to App's single keyboard dispatcher — the reader adds
43	  no window listener — and ignore commands without a ready, matching displayed
44	  visit (including expansion/details commands during loading). They dispatch
45	  after the existing editor/IME/modifier/
46	  editable/overlay guards. Native Enter/Space button activation is preserved
47	  (one activation toggles expansion once, never a mailbox action), and the
48	  existing `e`/`Shift+U` action contracts work from the new message-toggle
49	  focus: a message toggle is the reader's navigation context, not a toolbar
50	  action button, so the conversation-level shortcuts remain usable there while
51	  every other focused button/link keeps the generic exclusion. Toolbar,
52	  editor/IME, overlay, capability, read-only, and stale-target guards are
53	  unchanged.
54	- **Reading progress across foreground loading:** the outgoing visit's
55	  viewport-relative scroll anchor is captured before any DOM teardown —
56	  including the foreground null/loading transition where the conversation is
57	  cleared before the next detail arrives — and retained through loading/error
58	  without being overwritten by the empty/loading DOM. Returning to a visit
59	  restores the exact scroll offset and viewport-relative message geometry, and
60	  revisit focus does not reveal-scroll over the restored offset (initial entry
61	  and explicit N/P still reveal the focused header as needed). When teardown
62	  removes reader-owned message focus, loading parks it on the persistent article,
63	  not BODY, without overriding toolbar, rail, overlay, or outside focus (including
64	  focus moved before delayed work runs). An immediate A-ready → B-loading →
65	  A-ready reversal restores A's message focus independently of the last loaded
66	  data key, unless the user moved to another surface.
67	- **Conversation movement:** Inbox-origin reader `J/K` moves the reader cursor
68	  through the originating Inbox's current ready snapshot resolved against the
69	  current `openRef` (previous context ordering for a removed cursor, no wrap),
70	  without moving hidden list focus and without recapturing the entry origin.
71	  Activity-origin reader `J/K` is a strict no-op: no navigation, no hidden-focus
72	  mutation, no invented ordering of duplicate operation references, and no extra
73	  `getConversation` calls; `N/P/O` still work there. Reader ArrowUp/ArrowDown
74	  retain native behavior instead of switching threads; list arrow aliases remain.
75	- **Back/Escape restoration:** the original entry focus, account-scoped
76	  ordering, and non-null list anchor are captured only at the initial
77	  list-to-reader entry. Back (Escape/Close) restores the ORIGINAL entry thread
78	  and best anchor with the fallback chain: surviving entry reference → next
79	  surviving neighbor from the entry ordering → previous → first valid row →
80	  empty state. An Activity-origin Back reopens Activity without erasing the
81	  saved underlying Inbox anchor; explicit Inbox navigation keeps the list's own
82	  current focus instead.
83	- **Actions target the current open thread only.** Archive/read/reply use the
84	  CURRENT loaded open conversation; the saved origin is never an action target.
85	  Existing stale-request/late-receipt guards and request tokens are retained.
86	  Inbox archive auto-advance captures account-scoped ACTION-TIME ordering before
87	  the archive, then selects the next surviving neighbor, otherwise the previous,
88	  without wrapping. This is separate from frozen Back entry ordering and J/K
89	  cursor resolution (`mailbox.focusedSummary` deliberately remains the original
90	  entry focus). An Activity-origin reader never advances into unrelated Inbox
91	  mail.
92	- **Participant details and context.** Each message exposes a native
93	  `<details>` disclosure with the complete known From/To addresses and sent
94	  timestamp; unknown Cc/Bcc and other headers are omitted, never fabricated.
95	  Participant names/addresses are keyboard-focusable context controls separate
96	  from the expansion toggle (no nested buttons). The active message's sender is
97	  the baseline reader contact; participant hover and keyboard focus each
98	  temporarily override it, keyboard focus wins, and exit (leave/blur, disclosure
99	  dismissal, message change, close) restores the baseline. Overrides are
100	  identity-qualified by conversation reference + message ID in App, so late
101	  blur/leave events, loading, removals, and account changes cannot leak a stale
102	  contact. Direct focus on a new message's participant preserves its valid
103	  identity-matching override across the active-message handoff instead of
104	  accidentally clearing it. A visible "Reply targets the latest message from …" label sits near
105	  Prepare reply so focusing an older message cannot imply a different reply
106	  target.
107	- **Copy controls (copy-only BROWSE-15 portion):** separately labelled
108	  copy-name (only when a display name is known) and copy-email buttons in
109	  `ContactPane.vue`, reachable by hover and keyboard. Activation uses
110	  `navigator.clipboard.writeText` only on explicit activation and reports
111	  success, failure, or unavailable-clipboard honestly via `role="status"`, with
112	  the text staying selectable for manual copy. Outcomes reset when the displayed
113	  identity/context changes or a new copy activates; asynchronous results publish
114	  only for the matching identity/context and newest activation, so reversed
115	  completions cannot replace the newer result. Copying never triggers a draft,
116	  navigation, or any mailbox write, and adds no native permission.
117	- **Safety unchanged:** bodies render exclusively through text interpolation —
118	  no `v-html`, no HTML/Markdown processing, no remote assets; hostile markup
119	  stays literal text (asserted in real Chrome). Retained/incomplete/header
120	  checks, `unsupportedReason`/`contextComplete` disclosures, draft lifecycle and
121	  close protection, permission gates, no-auto-read, and overlay inertness are
122	  preserved.
123	- **Reader surface:** the reader is a bounded flex surface with its own content
124	  scroller and a persistent toolbar/Back affordance; the toolbar stays fixed
125	  while content scrolls beneath it (asserted with real layout geometry in
126	  Chrome). The 1000px Contact breakpoint and covered-surface inertness are
127	  preserved, including the wide contact column being inert while a utility
128	  drawer overlays it.

131	
132	- Escape precedence inside the reader: an open message-details disclosure is
133	  dismissed before the reader closes; utility drawers and the narrow Contact
134	  disclosure keep their existing earlier precedence.
135	- The participant context displays the participant's display name when present

Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- persona-feature-engineer: Implement scoped features with focused tests and before-and-after verification evidence (Tools: All tools)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)
- tldraw-offline: Use proactively when a task touches the user's tldraw offline canvas app, (which they may refer to as tldraw, or tldraw desktop, or reference a .tldraw or .tldr file), but use this IF it's a complex, long-running task. This subagent can edit the canvas as well as add durable scripts to canvases that change their behavior. Be concise with your instructions, the subagent has access to all the context it needs. Do not ask it to verify. (Tools: Bash, Read, Write, Edit, MultiEdit)

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for reading and writing to .pen files and gives you tools to be an expert design generator and validator specifically for web and mobile applications and websites.

- IMPORTANT: The contents of the .pen files are encrypted and can be only access via the "pencil" MCP tools. DO NOT use "Read" or "Grep" tools to read contents of .pen files.
- IMPORTANT: Make sure to ONLY use the "pencil" MCP tools when reading or searching contents of .pen files (batch_get) and making changes inside .pen files (batch_design).
- IMPORTANT: Always follow the tool definitions and formats for the "pencil" MCP tools.

Available tools:
- "get_editor_state()": Start with this tool if you are aware of the current editor state. Use this tool to determine in the beginning of a task, to understand what is the currently active .pen file you want to work on and the current user selection in it and other essential context information.
- "open_document(filePathOrNew)": When there is no active editor opened, pass 'new' to create an empty .pen file or if the user explicitly ask to open a specific .pen file use its path to open it.
- "get_guidelines(topic=code|table|tailwind|landing-page|slides|design-system|mobile-app|web-app)": This tool returns design guidelines and rules for working with .pen files. Only use it if you need one of the available topics for your design task. ONLY use the topics defined in the tool's description.
- "get_style_guide_tags": Use this tool after using "get_guidelines" for additional design inspiration with "get_style_guide".
- "get_style_guide(tags, name)": This tool returns a style guide to be used in the ongoing design task based on a set of relevant tags or a specific style guide by name. Ask for a style guide when designing screens, websites, apps or dashboards and not working with a design system already.
- "batch_get(patterns, nodeIds)": Retrieve nodes by searching for matching patterns or by reading node ids in batches. Use this for discovering and understand .pen files.
- "batch_design(operations)": Use it when designing with .pen files to execute multiple insert/copy/update/replace/move/delete/image operations in a single call. IMPORTANT: MAKE SURE TO FOLLOW THE OPERATION SYNTAX DEFINED IN THE TOOL'S DESCRIPTION. Aim for maximum 25 operations per call—enough to make meaningful progress without overwhelming the system. Available operations (used as a small script where every line a single operation call):
	- Insert: foo=I("parent", { ... })
	- Copy: baz=C("nodeid", "parent", { ...})
	- Replace: foo2=R("nodeid1/nodeid2", {...})
	- Update: U(foo+"/nodeid", {...})
	- Delete: D("dfFAeg2")
	- Move: M("nodeid3", "parent", 2)
	- Generate image - G("baz", "ai", "...")
- "snapshot_layout": Check the current layout structure of an .pen file. Use this tool to examine the computed layout rectangles of each node in an .pen file, to decide where to insert new nodes.
- "get_screenshot": This tool returns a screenshot of a node in a .pen file. Use this tool to periodically validate design visually.
- "get_variables": Use this tool to extract the current state of variables and themes defined in this .pen file.
- "set_variables": Use this tool to add or update variables in this .pen file.
- "find_empty_space_on_canvas": Find empty space on the canvas in a .pen file for a given direction and desired size.
- "search_all_unique_properties": Recursively search for all unique properties on the entire node tree on provided parent ids.
- "replace_all_matching_properties": Recursively replace all matching properties on the entire node tree on provided parent ids.

1	# Product
2	
3	## Register
4	
5	product
6	
7	## Users
8	
9	Initially a single person: the author, dogfooding a single-account desktop client (macOS first) against their own Gmail inbox in focused, keyboard-first sessions. They move through a high volume of mail quickly, want to reach "done" on each conversation, and need to trust that every action (archive, bulk processing, undo, send) did exactly what it claimed. The provider's own client remains the fallback.
10	
11	Longer term: technically capable people who want to compose their own email workflow (custom views, triage signals, commands, automations), manually or with an agent, without rebuilding sync, credentials, or send safety.
12	
13	The primary task on most screens is triage: scan the list, open a conversation, decide, act, move on.
14	
15	## Product Purpose
16	
17	A composable email client: a trusted mail engine (sync, safe rendering, credentials, action execution) with replaceable signals, views, commands, and workflows on top. It ships an opinionated reference experience, a compact Superhuman-style browsing and keyboard flow, rather than a blank toolkit.
18	
19	The near-term goal is a complete, trustworthy inbox-processing session. Strategic scope is set by `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` and `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`; this file does not expand it.
20	
21	Success looks like: the author processes their inbox faster and with more confidence than in their previous client, and every automated or bulk action is previewable, reported honestly (including partial success and "outcome unknown"), and undoable where undo is real.
22	
23	## Brand Personality
24	
25	**Focused, precise, trustworthy.**
26	
27	- **Focused:** the interface recedes so the mail and the next decision are what's on screen. Dense, quiet, few competing elements.
28	- **Precise:** exact states, exact counts, exact wording. No vague "something went wrong", no rounded-off truth about what happened.
29	- **Trustworthy:** the client never overstates what it did. Pending, failed, partial, and ambiguous outcomes are visible and distinct. Automation shows its work before it acts.
30	
31	Voice is terse and factual: short labels, plain verbs, no exclamation marks, no cheerleading.
32	
33	## Anti-references
34	
35	- **Gmail-web clutter:** toolbars of rarely-used icons, chrome competing with content, permanent competing panels.
36	- **"AI magic" email products:** AI destinations, sparkle icons, generated summaries presented as fact, fabricated contact enrichment, automation that acts without a preview.
37	- **Superhuman feature-parity clone:** Superhuman is the visual and interaction reference for browsing (layout, density, type, keyboard feel), and close look parity there is a goal. Features and workflows are our own; don't import Superhuman's product scope or claim verified behavioral parity.
38	- **Generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics:** card stacks and grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration or motion.
39	- **Optimistic UI that lies:** "Done" before the provider confirmed, silent retries of ambiguous sends, dead controls that look actionable.
40	
41	## Design Principles
42	
43	1. **Honest state over smooth feel.** When speed and truthfulness conflict, show the truth. Every action has a visible pending, success, partial, failed, or unknown state. Show evidence and coverage, including unknown and retained facts.
44	2. **Keyboard first, mouse welcome.** Every core triage path is reachable and discoverable from the keyboard; pointer interaction is supported, never required.
45	3. **Content is the interface.** Chrome stays quiet and compact so the list and the conversation dominate. Add UI only when it earns its space in the triage loop; reuse established commands, navigation and recovery surfaces before adding new ones.
46	4. **Preview before power.** Bulk actions, automations, and agent-proposed changes show what they will do before they do it, and report exactly what they did after. Focus, bulk selection and message identity stay separate concepts.
47	5. **Opinionated defaults, replaceable parts.** Ship one strong way of working; design surfaces so views, signals, and commands can be swapped without breaking the core experience.
48	
49	Standing constraints: ordinary reading stays local and non-mutating; message content renders as safe literal plain text; drafts stay local-only.
50	
51	## Accessibility & Inclusion
52	
53	Not a formal priority at this stage; no WCAG conformance target or certification is implied. Keyboard operability and visible focus remain required because they are core to the keyboard-first model. Don't regress behavior that already exists (explicit action labels, editable/IME shortcut protection, reduced-motion alternatives, selection/outcome announcements). The existing desktop/contact breakpoints remain authoritative; no new mobile UI. Revisit if the audience expands beyond the author.
54

It never separates rows (the list has no row borders). The old #3b3936 survives as the quieter `rule` token for structure inside a pane, only in the reader (toolbar and message rules) and inside drawers (Activity and draft rows, group detail, Account panel, Reminders fieldset), so those surfaces keep their tone until a reader reference is captured. `focus-accent` stays at the committed #bba5ed; the capture reads about #bfa1f6, which is within capture and color-profile noise.
224:11. **Global button style.** Done (polish pass). The `button` defaults are zero-specificity (`:where()`), so every component class keeps its own look. The default is a ghost: transparent, Paper White, 4px radius, `4px 8px` (24px tall at 12px, the old chip's hit target), Lifted Charcoal on hover, Focus Stone on press, 0.45 opacity when disabled, and the 2px Dusk Lavender focus ring at a 1px offset. The selection bar, the action notice's Undo, Load more, the search form and the reader toolbar are ghost text buttons. Bordered `button-utility` chips (Lifted Charcoal, 1px Seam, `3px 8px`) appear only inside utility drawers, the modal attachment chooser, recovery banners (`.recovery-banner`: draft-close recovery, inbox/account load errors, the reader's navigation error, the header's saved-split error) and the synthetic workspace strip. Fields follow "Inputs / Fields": a Seam border that shifts to Dusk Lavender (plus a 1px inner outline) on keyboard focus, Smoke placeholders (4.76:1 on Lifted Charcoal) and a lavender ring on native checkboxes.
226:13. **In-flow bars.** Done (polish pass). Every bar is borderless Body type with its text on the 50px content inset and 6px block padding. The lines that come and go with triage keys (the Selection bar, the single-slot Action notice and the command-error alert) now live in a bottom dock of the list column (`.list-dock`) instead of above the list, so x, e and z never move a row. Measured at 1280×800 (Gmail preview): the first row stays at y=126 (real clock) or y=78 (Today clock) through x, x, Clear, e and z; before, it moved 126 → 186.9 → 162.8 → 156. The dock keeps one 36px line reserved and grows upward into the list viewport (selection: 56px). If that shrink would clip the focused row, the list scrolls just enough to keep it whole. The static context lines (Starred/Done coverage, draft-close recovery) stay above the list, because they belong to the destination rather than to an action. The reader's selection-scope note is a borderless line in the reader.
227:14. **Type scale and dates.** Done (2026-11-07 typeset pass). The shell type is semantic tokens on `:root`: `--type-headline` 1rem, `--type-body` 0.75rem, `--type-count` 0.6875rem, `--type-mono` 0.85rem, weights 400/600 only (`--weight-regular`, `--weight-strong`). `.app-main` sets Body as the shell default, so the rail, contact pane, notices, drawers, the reader chrome and form controls are 12px instead of an inherited 16px or ad hoc 0.8/0.85/0.9/0.95/1.1rem. Shell h2 is Headline; h3/h4 and in-panel drawer headings are Title; the reader subject is Headline at 600. Row dates follow the Label rules below and are deterministic (no default-locale dependence: the old `30 Sept 2001` vs `Sep 30, 2001` rendered-layout gate now passes under any `LANG`). Rows carry `<time datetime>` plus the full date as the title; reader message times are full dates with `datetime`. The rendered larger-text gate expected the compact action disclosure at a 25px root font (was 23px) after this pass, and at 34.5px (expanded at 30px) after the rail/contact pass, since the fixed-px rail and contact pane leave the list wider at every text size.

The command overlay and the attachment chooser are on the scale (gaps 12 and 14). Remaining: the Reminders time input still takes a typed ISO value; it is an input, not a display.

The reader's type is on the shell scale (typeset pass: Headline subject at 600, 12px message chrome, full dates, Mono body), but its layout and colours keep their current tokens until a reader reference is captured.

1	# Product
2	
3	## Register
4	
5	product
6	
7	## Users
8	
9	Initially a single person: the author, dogfooding a single-account desktop client (macOS first) against their own Gmail inbox in focused, keyboard-first sessions. They move through a high volume of mail quickly, want to reach "done" on each conversation, and need to trust that every action (archive, bulk processing, undo, send) did exactly what it claimed. The provider's own client remains the fallback.
10	
11	Longer term: technically capable people who want to compose their own email workflow (custom views, triage signals, commands, automations), manually or with an agent, without rebuilding sync, credentials, or send safety.
12	
13	The primary task on most screens is triage: scan the list, open a conversation, decide, act, move on.
14	
15	## Product Purpose
16	
17	A composable email client: a trusted mail engine (sync, safe rendering, credentials, action execution) with replaceable signals, views, commands, and workflows on top. It ships an opinionated reference experience, a compact Superhuman-style browsing and keyboard flow, rather than a blank toolkit.
18	
19	The near-term goal is a complete, trustworthy inbox-processing session. Strategic scope is set by `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` and `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`; this file does not expand it.
20	
21	Success looks like: the author processes their inbox faster and with more confidence than in their previous client, and every automated or bulk action is previewable, reported honestly (including partial success and "outcome unknown"), and undoable where undo is real.
22	
23	## Brand Personality
24	
25	**Focused, precise, trustworthy.**
26	
27	- **Focused:** the interface recedes so the mail and the next decision are what's on screen. Dense, quiet, few competing elements.
28	- **Precise:** exact states, exact counts, exact wording. No vague "something went wrong", no rounded-off truth about what happened.
29	- **Trustworthy:** the client never overstates what it did. Pending, failed, partial, and ambiguous outcomes are visible and distinct. Automation shows its work before it acts.
30	
31	Voice is terse and factual: short labels, plain verbs, no exclamation marks, no cheerleading.
32	
33	## Anti-references
34	
35	- **Gmail-web clutter:** toolbars of rarely-used icons, chrome competing with content, permanent competing panels.
36	- **"AI magic" email products:** AI destinations, sparkle icons, generated summaries presented as fact, fabricated contact enrichment, automation that acts without a preview.
37	- **Superhuman feature-parity clone:** Superhuman is the visual and interaction reference for browsing (layout, density, type, keyboard feel), and close look parity there is a goal. Features and workflows are our own; don't import Superhuman's product scope or claim verified behavioral parity.
38	- **Generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics:** card stacks and grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration or motion.
39	- **Optimistic UI that lies:** "Done" before the provider confirmed, silent retries of ambiguous sends, dead controls that look actionable.
40	
41	## Design Principles
42	
43	1. **Honest state over smooth feel.** When speed and truthfulness conflict, show the truth. Every action has a visible pending, success, partial, failed, or unknown state. Show evidence and coverage, including unknown and retained facts.
44	2. **Keyboard first, mouse welcome.** Every core triage path is reachable and discoverable from the keyboard; pointer interaction is supported, never required.
45	3. **Content is the interface.** Chrome stays quiet and compact so the list and the conversation dominate. Add UI only when it earns its space in the triage loop; reuse established commands, navigation and recovery surfaces before adding new ones.
46	4. **Preview before power.** Bulk actions, automations, and agent-proposed changes show what they will do before they do it, and report exactly what they did after. Focus, bulk selection and message identity stay separate concepts.
47	5. **Opinionated defaults, replaceable parts.** Ship one strong way of working; design surfaces so views, signals, and commands can be swapped without breaking the core experience.
48	
49	Standing constraints: ordinary reading stays local and non-mutating; message content renders as safe literal plain text; drafts stay local-only.
50	
51	## Accessibility & Inclusion
52	
53	Not a formal priority at this stage; no WCAG conformance target or certification is implied. Keyboard operability and visible focus remain required because they are core to the keyboard-first model. Don't regress behavior that already exists (explicit action labels, editable/IME shortcut protection, reduced-motion alternatives, selection/outcome announcements). The existing desktop/contact breakpoints remain authoritative; no new mobile UI. Revisit if the audience expands beyond the author.
54

content.text:
**Status: complete.** All five steps are implemented and left uncommitted in the working tree. `pnpm test`, `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm build` pass. Two real-Chrome reader tests fail or time out, but both fail the same way on unmodified HEAD, so this change did not cause them.

## What changed, per step

1. **Prefetch the neighbour.** `useMailbox.ts` gains `prefetchConversation(ref)` and a cache keyed `accountId:conversationId`, with at most 3 entries and a 30s TTL (`DETAIL_CACHE_MAX`, `DETAIL_CACHE_TTL_MS`).
   - App arms one prefetch once the reader is `ready`, in the direction of the last move (+1 by default, reset when the reader closes). It uses the same `readerNavigates` condition as J/K, so Activity-, Reminders- and Trash-origin readers never prefetch.
   - A new `openNeighbor(ref)` is used by J/K and the chevrons. On a cache hit it swaps in synchronously and then revalidates through the existing `loadDetail(..., background=true)` path. On a miss it joins an in-flight prefetch for the same target instead of issuing a duplicate request. Archive auto-advance and recent-mail opens still use `openConversationByRef` and are unchanged.
   - Prefetch never writes, never marks read, never shows an error, and runs at most one at a time. Only the latest wanted target is queued.
   - The whole cache is invalidated at the start of `refresh()` (covers sync, reload, retry, subscription events), when `mutationsAllowed()` succeeds (every single, group, undo and retry mutation), and in `closeReader()` (which account change, disconnect, context change and search also call). In-flight results are fenced by a `detailEpoch` counter.
2. **Delayed loading state.** `READER_LOADING_DELAY_MS = 120` is exported. J/K keeps `conversation = null` and `detailState = 'loading'`, so every existing action guard behaves as before. A new display-only `heldConversation` ref keeps the previous thread on screen. A held thread has no action target. A second J keeps the original 120ms deadline. `detailToken` still discards stale and out-of-order responses.
3. **Real identity.** `ReaderView` has a new `loadingIdentity` prop, filled from the list row for `openRef` (subject, sender, date). It shows the subject, a sender and date line, then a quiet "Loading conversation…" line. It never shows the held or incoming body. `ContactPane` has a new `loading` prop, so it shows nothing instead of "No correspondent information is available." while loading. App passes the list row's sender as the contact during loading.
4. **Header actions stay mounted.** Mark done, read toggle, files, prepare reply and the in-message reply glyph stay mounted whenever `openRef` is set, and are disabled unless the detail is `ready`. The prev/next chevrons were already always mounted. All `data-test` ids, visually-hidden text, the inline fallback and the bulk-selection text controls are preserved. Held content ignores message toggles, details and N/P/O.
5. **Focus and scroll.** `.reader-scroll` is reset to 0 on a conversation switch when the target visit has no saved anchor. Returning to the same conversation still restores its anchor. The existing focus logic now moves focus once to the new newest toggle. Focus stays on the old toggle while content is held, and sits on the reader container only while the loading presentation shows.

## Files changed
- `src/composables/useMailbox.ts`, `src/App.vue`, `src/components/ReaderView.vue`, `src/components/ContactPane.vue`
- `src/assets/style.css` (loading identity styles only; no motion)
- `tests/reader-navigation.smooth.test.ts` (new, 23 tests)
- `tests/app.component.test.ts`, `tests/discovery.component.test.ts`, `tests/reminders.navigation.test.ts`, `tests/reader.rendered.test.ts` (deliberate updates, listed below)
- `src/lib/ipc/browser-fake.ts` is not in the diff. The scratch latency was added and reverted; `git status` confirms it.

## Existing tests I changed
- **`app.component` "does not archive the previous conversation while the next detail is loading":** the archive toggle now exists but is `disabled`, so the assertion changed from "absent" to "disabled".
- **`app.component` "keeps a stale delayed detail…":** the delay is now a gate on the prefetched read-02. It asserts the held, non-actionable state inside the window and the loading presentation after it. The stale-discard assertions are kept.
- **`discovery` "revalidates targets across slow reader navigation":** opens read-03 and presses K to the uncached read-02, because J would now hit the cache. It still asserts that the palette cannot mutate the previous thread.
- **`discovery` "recovers surviving focus…":** asserts the first call after K is read-01, since a prefetch may follow it.
- **`reminders.navigation`:** the call log now includes the legitimate prefetch of the neighbour, asserted explicitly.
- **`reader.rendered` (two delayed-J tests):** a `notify()` drops the cache so J really loads, waits are raised past 120ms, and the `.reader-subject === null` assertion now checks `reader-loading-subject` plus no `reader-messages`.

## Checks
- `pnpm vitest run` (full suite): **46 files passed, 4 skipped; 739 passed, 32 skipped**.
- `pnpm typecheck`: passes. `pnpm build`: passes.
- Mutation checks: I temporarily broke the hold, refresh invalidation, mutation invalidation, scroll reset, header unmount, toggle guard and the ContactPane loading branch. The new tests failed each time. I then confirmed the source files were restored to their final state.
- Real Chrome, using Playwright's Chromium via the opt-in env variable:
  - `discovery.rendered` 16/16, `disclosure-focus.rendered` 1/1, `inbox-list.rendered-layout` 2/2.
  - `reader.rendered`: 11 of 13 pass. Two fail:
    - "directly focused participant override…" fails identically on unmodified HEAD, which I extracted with `git archive` into the scratchpad.
    - "action-time neighbor ordering" times out at the 5s limit when run after the other tests. It passed at 4999ms on HEAD, and passes alone in about 1.1s on my code.

## Frame timelines (browser fixture, per-frame sampling)
In `before` / `after`, "J" means one J press; "cached" means the neighbour was prefetched. `Icons` counts the archive/files/reply glyphs. In the real run the prev/next chevrons were also mounted throughout.

| Scenario | t after J | Subject | Body | Icons (disabled) | Contact pane | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before, 250ms | 9ms | none | 318px to 40px | 3 to 0 | "No correspondent information…" | reader container |
| before, 250ms | 260ms | thread 2 | full | 3 (0) | Ada | newest toggle |
| before, 60ms | 7ms to 73ms | empty for 66ms | | 3 to 0 | no-info text | container |
| after, cached | 10ms | thread 2 | full, no empty frame | 3 (0) | Ada | one move, toggle to toggle |
| after, response at ~83ms (100ms latency) | 3ms | thread 1 held | full | 3 (3 disabled) | Ada | stays on the old toggle |
| after, response at ~83ms | 83ms | thread 2 | full | 3 (0) | Ada | one move |
| after, slow miss (400ms) | 3ms | thread 1 held | full | 3 (3 disabled) | Ada | old toggle |
| after, slow miss (400ms) | 129ms | thread 3 + sender + date | loading line | 3 (3 disabled) | Ada (list row) | reader container |
| after, slow miss (400ms) | 379ms | thread 3 | full | 3 (0) | Ada | one move |
| after, rapid J J J (250ms) | 88ms to 263ms | thread 4 only | | disabled, mounted | Ada | container, then thread 4 toggle |

The rapid J J J run went held, loading with thread 4's identity, then thread 4. It never rendered thread 2 or 3 again.

The fixture's contact is "Ada Fixture" for every thread, so the contact column doesn't show a list-sender versus no-info difference by name. The "no information" text is gone during loading, and the tests assert it.

## Evidence paths
Everything is under `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-sofianebebert-workspace-worktrees-email-os-t3-8289bc5f/c76d33d1-bfb7-485b-a7f9-1da77be42a31/scratchpad/evidence/jk-smooth/`.
- `before/` has `before-slow250-timeline.json`, `before-fast60-timeline.json` and `before-rapid-jjj-timeline.json`, plus `before-slow250-mid-load.png` (the empty frame and the false contact text) and `before-slow250-after-load.png`.
- `after/` has `after-cached-250`, `after-fast-miss-within-window`, `after-slow400-shots`, `after-slow250-miss`, `after-fast60-miss` and `after-rapid-jjj` timelines. Screenshots: `after-slow400-shots-held-60ms.png`, `after-slow400-shots-loading-identity-160ms.png` (target subject, sender, date, quiet loading line, disabled icons, list sender in the contact pane) and `after-slow400-shots-arrived.png`.
- Harness: `.../scratchpad/pw/smooth.mjs`. I used no video, and the dev server on port 5240 is stopped.

## Prefetch budget, for the Gmail quota decision
- **After a reader becomes ready:** 1 extra `getConversation` for the neighbour in the last-move direction.
- **Per J/K on a cache hit:** 1 revalidation call, plus 1 prefetch of the next neighbour. That is 2 calls per move. Before this change it was 1.
- **Per J/K on a miss or an adopted prefetch:** 1 call, plus 1 prefetch after arrival.
- **At most 1 prefetch in flight.** Superseded wants are dropped, so there is no queue.
- **Each refresh while a reader is open:** about 1 extra neighbour fetch, because the cache is invalidated and re-armed. This includes window-focus and subscription refreshes.
- **Cache:** 3 entries, 30s TTL, in memory only. Nothing is stored on disk and nothing is written to the mailbox.

## Risks and limits
- During the 120ms hold, the held thread's header icons are disabled and dimmed to 0.45 opacity, so a short flicker is possible on a mid-latency fetch. The icons stay mounted, so nothing shifts layout. Keeping them visually enabled would need `aria-disabled` and click guards, which is a different decision.
- An in-flight prefetch is not aborted when you navigate. Its result goes into the cache only if the epoch is unchanged. A request already on the wire still completes, which is cheap and read-only.
- A background revalidation that fails after a cache hit shows the error state, the same as an existing background refresh does.
- The `reader.rendered` suite is opt-in and I ran it on macOS Chromium 1228. The `reader.rendered` failures and the borderline timeout above are also present on unmodified HEAD.

## Suggested DESIGN.md notes
- J/K never shows an empty reader. The previous conversation stays for up to 120ms and is never actionable. After that the loading presentation shows the target's subject, sender and date from the list row, plus one quiet "Loading conversation…" line. No motion.
- Header actions stay mounted and disabled while a conversation is not ready. They are never removed.
- The contact pane never claims "no information" while loading.
- Focus moves once, to the new newest-message toggle. Focus sits on the reader container only while the loading presentation shows. Scroll resets to the top on a first visit and restores on a revisit.
- Performance and quota: one read-only neighbour prefetch with a small in-memory cache, invalidated by any mailbox mutation or refresh.

No decisions are pending.
